group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
An 89-year-old man who still resides in the bungalow he built after returning from military service and who remains largely self-sufficient—he prepares his own breakfast, manages his medications, and tends a small vegetable garden—was brought to the emergency department by his adult grandson late this morning after three days of progressively deeper cough, scant rusty sputum, and fevers that peaked overnight high enough to drench the bedclothes; he insisted on skipping the acetaminophen his daughter offered so the hospital team could “see the numbers straight.” He observed that climbing the five steps from his porch required two pauses today and that he felt “winded just walking to the mailbox,” shortness of breath not present at baseline. Past history is notable for a left middle cerebral artery ischemic event four years ago that left a mild expressive aphasia now barely perceptible, and for chronic systolic dysfunction attributed to idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy with an ejection fraction of 30 % on an echocardiogram six months earlier; he takes carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, low-dose furosemide most mornings, and sacubitril-valsartan 24-26 mg twice daily with good refill adherence. He has never been told he has chronic kidney disease, cirrhosis, or any form of malignancy, and his last outpatient basic metabolic panel two months ago documented a creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL and sodium 139 mEq/L. He quit smoking cigarettes three decades ago after a 40 pack-year exposure, drinks one glass of red wine with Sunday dinner, and denies recreational drug use. Immunization records at his primary clinic confirm both pneumococcal formulations and this season’s influenza shot. He lives with his wife, does not receive home health aide services, and has never spent time in a skilled-nursing facility. The grandson drove him the 35 minute trip with windows cracked; no supplemental oxygen, nebulizers, intravenous fluids, or antipyretics were given en route. On arrival the patient sat bolt upright on the stretcher, lips pursed, speaking in brief phrases but clearly oriented to name, place, date, and current events. Skin appeared flushed and dry with poor axillary sweat; mucous membranes were tacky, and capillary refill remained under two seconds. Pre-intervention vital signs on ambient air at this sea-level institution revealed an oral temperature of 38.45 °C (101.2 °F), an irregular but rapid radial pulse that averaged 139 beats per minute over a full minute and was confirmed on three-lead monitoring as sinus tachycardia, a non-invasive right-arm blood pressure of 151/76 mm Hg verified manually, respirations counted at 63 breaths per minute with pronounced intercostal and suprasternal recruitment, and pulse oximetry fluctuating between 92 % and 94 %. Jugular venous contour was 4 cm above the sternal angle while upright—unchanged from cardiology notes—and there was trace bilateral ankle edema. Cardiac auscultation disclosed a crisp S1 and S2 with a soft third heart sound already documented previously, no new murmurs or pericardial rub. Pulmonary examination demonstrated coarse crackles throughout the right mid-zone and lower posterior lung field with bronchial breath sounds over the right apex, preserved resonance to percussion bilaterally, and no stony dullness or egophony at either costophrenic angle. Abdomen was scaphoid and nontender; the liver edge was not palpated below the costal margin, and no splenomegaly or shifting dullness was appreciated. Neurologic screen showed equal reactive pupils, intact extra-ocular movements, a mildly labored but fluent speech pattern identical to his previous baseline, and 5/5 strength in all extremities. A bedside glucometer prior to venous access read 157 mg/dL. Two large-bore peripheral lines were placed, flushed only with minimal saline to maintain patency, and venous samples together with a right radial arterial puncture were obtained within ten minutes of arrival—before any crystalloid, diuretic, antipyretic, antibiotic, vasodilator, or oxygen therapy was given. The basic metabolic panel returned sodium 169 mEq/L, potassium 3.9 mEq/L, chloride 115 mEq/L, bicarbonate 18 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 67 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, revealing severe hypernatremia and azotemia out of proportion to his preserved filtration baseline. Complete blood count demonstrated leukocytes 17.4 × 10⁹/L with 90 % segmented neutrophils, a striking hematocrit of 68 %, hemoglobin 22.1 g/dL, and platelets 255 × 10⁹/L, consistent with significant hemoconcentration. The arterial blood gas on room air revealed a pH of 7.16, PaCO₂ 22 mm Hg, PaO₂ 109 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 8 mEq/L, indicating a severe metabolic acidosis with partial respiratory alkalotic compensation yet preservation of oxygen tension. Serum lactate measured 3.1 mmol/L. High-sensitivity troponin was below the assay threshold, and NT-proBNP returned at 3,500 pg/mL, similar to prior clinic values. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph obtained fifteen minutes into the visit, before any therapeutic intervention, showed a dense consolidation occupying the right upper and middle lobes with air bronchograms, sharp costophrenic angles, and a cardiac silhouette unchanged from films six months earlier; no layering fluid or meniscus was visualized. Twelve-lead electrocardiography displayed sinus tachycardia at 138 bpm with nonspecific ST-T flattening but no acute ischemic pattern compared with a tracing on file from last year. Two peripheral sets of blood cultures, an induced sputum specimen for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigens for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila, and a multiplex respiratory viral PCR panel were dispatched to the laboratory before any empiric antibiotics or intravenous therapy were ordered. Up to the moment this narrative is documented he remains seated upright on 21 % inspired oxygen, has received no intravenous fluids beyond the saline used to lock the lines, no diuretics, no vasoactive drugs, no bronchodilators, and no antipyretics, such that every vital sign, laboratory datum, and imaging finding above reflects his untreated physiologic state on presentation.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) adds demographic, comorbidity, examination, and investigation points from presentation.
- Demographics: a man scores his age in years = 89. He lives at home, so nursing-home residence adds 0.
- Comorbidities: systolic heart failure = 10; cerebrovascular disease (prior ischemic stroke) = 10. No malignancy, liver disease, or chronic renal disease = 0 each.
- Examination: respiratory rate 63/min (≥30) = 20; pulse 139/min (≥125) = 10. He is oriented, systolic BP 151 mm Hg is not <90, and temperature 38.45 °C is neither <35 nor ≥40: 0 each.
- Investigations: arterial pH 7.16 (<7.35) = 30; BUN 67 mg/dL (≥30) = 20. Sodium 169 is not <130 mEq/L, glucose 157 is not ≥250 mg/dL, hematocrit 68% is not <30%, room-air PaO₂ 109 is not <60 mm Hg, and there is no pleural effusion: 0 each.
Total = 89 + 10 + 10 + 20 + 10 + 30 + 20 = 189.
Final answer: 189
